text: Chapters one and two built the skeleton of a flow: triggers, variables, data pills, conditions, and loops. None of that skeleton actually changes a record on its own. The real work happens in actions, and in practice, the overwhelming majority of flows lean on just three built-in actions.

Create Record inserts a brand-new row on whatever table you point it at. You pick the table — Incident, Change Request, a custom table, anything — then map its field values using the same data-pill mechanism from lesson five: a value pulled from the trigger record, from an earlier step's output, or a static value you type directly. Create Record always produces something new.

Update Record modifies a record that already exists, most often the record that triggered the flow in the first place, since that record is automatically available as a data pill. A flow triggered on Incident update might use it to set the assignment group based on category. It can also target a record looked up elsewhere in the flow, not only the trigger record.

Course three of this path covered the real Notification mechanism — admin-configured email templates tied to tables and events. Flow Designer's notification action lets a flow fire one of those existing notifications, or send a direct message, as a single step. No new Notification record has to be built from scratch for every flow that needs to email someone.

This is why course three wasn't wasted effort — Flow Designer builds on top of the existing notification infrastructure rather than replacing it. A flow routes data into the message, and the platform's existing delivery mechanism handles the rest.

Picture a realistic flow: an Asset Request is submitted, Create Record opens a formal fulfillment ticket, Update Record marks the original submission as in progress, and a notification action emails the requester to confirm it was received. Each action does exactly one job — the flow's value comes from chaining them in the right order with the right data feeding each one.
Create, Update, Notify — the actual backbone most flows are built from. Next up: Approval Actions, where a flow pauses entirely and waits on a real human decision before it can continue.
